lead: This unit explains how a blockchain network with no boss reaches one agreed history: peers find each other and gossip, miners order transactions, and a consensus rule decides which block wins. After it you can trace one transaction from wallet to confirmed block, compare Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, Proof of Elapsed Time and round robin, and tell a soft fork from a hard fork.
about: Unit 3 is about how thousands of machines that do not trust each other end up holding the same ledger. Chapter 3.1 shows how peers find each other and gossip data. Chapter 3.2 follows one transaction from wallet to confirmed block and shows what miners actually do. Chapter 3.3 steps back and classifies the consensus families. Chapters 3.4 and 3.5 take the two big ones, Proof of Work and Proof of Stake, with their puzzles, rewards and attacks. Chapter 3.6 covers the lighter options used in permissioned chains, Proof of Elapsed Time and round robin. Chapter 3.7 closes with forks, the visible evidence of disagreement about rules. Read 3.1 and 3.2 first; every later chapter assumes a node broadcasts and a block is validated.

chapters.idea: A blockchain network is a set of equal nodes that find each other without a server and then spread every new transaction by gossip.
chapters.depth: Define peer, node and overlay network. Compare three architectures: client-server (one central server), pure peer-to-peer (every node equal), and hybrid (a few supernodes or bootstrap servers help, as Bitcoin's DNS seeds do). Short history: Napster, Gnutella, BitTorrent, then Bitcoin as the first P2P network carrying money. Working, step by step: join using a hardcoded seed or DNS seed, handshake (version/verack), learn addresses with getaddr/addr gossip, then flood data. Network discovery: bootstrap nodes, DNS seeds, peer address exchange, and structured lookup in a distributed hash table (DHT). Types of P2P in blockchain: unstructured (flooding with time-to-live, Bitcoin), structured (DHT keys), hybrid. Security measures: encrypted transport, signed messages, peer scoring and banning, many diverse connections to defeat an eclipse attack, limits on message size and hop count. Name Bitcoin and Ethereum as examples. One line: P2P crypto exchanges and P2P marketplaces are trading venues, not network topologies.

figure.title: Discovery from a bootstrap node
figure.aria: A bootstrap node hands out addresses, and each new peer then connects to further peers, so the graph grows outward.

chapters.example: A network floods each message with fan-out 3 and time-to-live 3 hops. How many copies of one new transaction travel, and how many in the last round? Round 0: the origin sends 3 copies. Round 1: those 3 peers send 3 each, so 9. Round 2: 27. Total sent = 3 + 9 + 27 = 39 copies. If you also count the origin's own copy, 40. Duplicate detection means a peer that receives the same transaction twice forwards it only once, so the real number stays near 39 and does not explode.
chapters.trap: Treating a P2P exchange (a trading website) as a P2P network, or assuming peers are trusted because they are connected.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for nodes, networks and the block structure.
chapters.leave: The Bitcoin wire protocol message list to Unit 4; Ethereum's devp2p to Unit 5; hash pointers to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A transaction travels from a wallet through a mempool into a miner's candidate block, and the miner is paid for the ordering.
chapters.depth: Full life cycle: wallet builds the transaction, signs it with the sender's private key, broadcasts to peers. Receiving nodes check the signature, the scripts and that the coins are unspent, then keep it in the mempool. Fee = transaction size in bytes × fee rate in satoshi per byte, so bigger transactions cost more. Miners pick from the mempool highest fee rate first, build a candidate block, run the puzzle, and broadcast the finished block. Other nodes validate the block fully and add it; after each further block one more confirmation is added. Coinbase transaction and its maturity. Role of miners: ordering transactions, extending the chain, issuing new coins, collecting fees. Full nodes that do not mine still validate everything; miners without validating nodes are blind. Stale or orphan blocks. One line on transaction malleability, pointing to SegWit in Unit 4.

figure.title: Life of one transaction
figure.aria: A transaction moves from the wallet through broadcast and the mempool into a candidate block, and only after the puzzle and full validation does it become confirmed.

chapters.example: A mempool holds three transactions. T1: 250 bytes, fee 5000 satoshi. T2: 500 bytes, fee 15000 satoshi. T3: 1000 bytes, fee 10000 satoshi. Fee rates: T1 = 5000 ÷ 250 = 20 sat/byte; T2 = 15000 ÷ 500 = 30 sat/byte; T3 = 10000 ÷ 1000 = 10 sat/byte. A miner filling a block orders them T2, then T1, then T3. Total size 250 + 500 + 1000 = 1750 bytes, total fee 30000 satoshi, which gives 30000 ÷ 1750 ≈ 17.1 sat/byte for the block.
chapters.trap: Believing a transaction is final after one block, or that the fee is a fixed amount rather than size × fee rate.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for hashing and digital signatures; Unit 1 for what a block contains.
chapters.leave: Bitcoin script, SegWit formats and wallet types to Unit 4; gas and account nonces to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Consensus is the rule set that makes independent nodes agree on one ordered history even when some of them are faulty or dishonest.
chapters.depth: Define consensus and the three properties: agreement, validity, termination. Why it is hard: no central authority, network delay, messages lost, nodes may lie (Byzantine fault). Classify mechanisms: proof-based (Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, Proof of Elapsed Time, Proof of Authority), voting-based (PBFT, Raft, Paxos, Tendermint), round robin, and hybrids. Permissionless chains need Sybil resistance; permissioned chains can vote because members are known. Probabilistic finality (a block may still be replaced) versus deterministic finality (decided at once). Fault tolerance: crash faults need n ≥ 2f + 1; Byzantine faults need n ≥ 3f + 1 and a quorum of 2f + 1, where n is the number of nodes and f the number of faulty ones. The 51% attack in one paragraph. Some syllabi write consensus algorithm or consensus protocol for the same thing.

figure.aria: The consensus families branch into proof-based, voting-based and round robin, and each branch lists its named mechanisms.

chapters.example: A permissioned network has n = 7 nodes and can tolerate f = 2 faulty ones. Check the Byzantine bound n ≥ 3f + 1: 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so 7 nodes are exactly enough. The quorum that must agree is 2f + 1 = 5 votes. If the answer had to tolerate f = 3, you would need n ≥ 3 × 3 + 1 = 10 nodes. For a public Proof of Work chain with 100 GH/s total, an attacker holding 40 GH/s has 40%, below the 51% needed to outrun the honest chain for long.
chapters.trap: Writing that all consensus is mining, or that Proof of Stake needs no Sybil resistance at all.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for public, private and consortium chains.
chapters.leave: The PoW puzzle to 3.4, PoS selection to 3.5, PoET and round robin to 3.6; the detailed Byzantine proof to a later course.

chapters.idea: Proof of Work makes a block expensive to produce by demanding a hash below a target, and difficulty keeps the rate steady.
chapters.depth: The puzzle: hash the block header (version, previous block hash, Merkle root, time, target bits, nonce) with SHA-256 and change the nonce until the output is numerically below the target. More leading zero hex digits means a smaller target and more expected tries: probability per try = 16 to the power minus z, expected tries = 16 to the power z, where z is the number of leading zero hex digits. Difficulty is target_1 divided by the current target, so higher difficulty means more work. Difficulty adjustment: every 2016 blocks, new difficulty = old difficulty × (2016 × 10 minutes) ÷ actual time taken, because one block per 10 minutes is the Bitcoin target. Mining hardware: CPU, then GPU, then FPGA, then ASIC. Mining pools: pool manager, shares, pay-per-share, pool hopping briefly. Attacks: 51% and double spending, selfish mining named only. Energy cost. Candidate block and the coinbase line.

figure.aria: Each extra leading zero hex digit multiplies the expected number of hash attempts by sixteen, so the curve rises steeply.

chapters.example: A target requires the first four hex digits of the 256-bit hash to be zero. Probability per try = 1 ÷ 16⁴ = 1 ÷ 65536, so the expected number of tries is 65536. A miner running at 2 × 10¹¹ hashes per second finds a block in about 65536 ÷ (2 × 10¹¹) ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ s if this were the whole network. Difficulty adjustment: a 2016-block window finishes in 12 days instead of the target 2016 × 10 min = 14 days. New difficulty = old × (14 ÷ 12) = old × 1.1667, so difficulty rises by about 16.7%.
chapters.trap: Saying more leading zeros make mining easier, or confusing difficulty with hash rate.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for SHA-256 and the block header; 3.3 for where PoW sits among the consensus types.
chapters.leave: Block rewards, halving and mining business economics to Unit 4; GHOST and uncle blocks to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Proof of Stake replaces computing power with locked coins, so a validator's chance to propose a block is proportional to its stake, and misbehaviour costs it coins.
chapters.depth: Core idea: the scarce resource is the native coin, not electricity. Selection by stake weight, with the alternatives coin-age-based and pure randomised selection. Validator deposits stake; if it signs two different blocks it is slashed, part of the stake is destroyed and it is removed. The nothing-at-stake problem and why slashing plus checkpoints answer it. Long-range attack. Probabilistic versus finality by checkpoint, so a block can be declared final. Delegated Proof of Stake in two lines: token holders vote for a small set of block producers. Advantages: low energy, cheap hardware, faster finality, smaller pool centralisation pressure. Disadvantages: rich get richer, cartel risk, security still needs a large honest majority of stake. Mention that Ethereum moved from PoW to PoS in 2022.

figure.title: Chance to propose is stake / total stake
figure.aria: Four validators hold different stakes, and each one's chance of being chosen to propose a block equals its share of the total stake.

chapters.example: Four validators hold 500, 300, 150 and 50 tokens, total 1000. Chance of proposing = stake ÷ 1000: A 50%, B 30%, C 15%, D 5%. In 100 blocks the expected counts are 50, 30, 15 and 5. Validator B double-signs two conflicting blocks and is slashed 5% of its 300 tokens = 15 tokens, so its stake falls to 285 and its chance falls to 28.5% of 1000 if nothing else changes.
chapters.trap: Claiming PoS removes all attacks, or that the largest stakeholder can never be voted out; slashing and checkpoints are the marks of a good answer.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 for proof-based consensus and Sybil resistance; Unit 2 for digital signatures.
chapters.leave: Ethereum's beacon chain, Casper FFG and validator client details to Unit 5; token economics to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Proof of Elapsed Time and round robin replace heavy computation with a fair turn rule, which suits permissioned chains.
chapters.depth: Proof of Elapsed Time: every validator asks a trusted timer for a random wait; the shortest wait wins the right to propose, and a signed proof shows the wait was genuine. Needs a trusted execution environment in hardware, so it is mainly Permissioned. Advantages: tiny energy use, fair spread, cheap hardware. Disadvantages: trust in the hardware maker, no protection if the hardware is broken, weak for public chains. Round robin: the leader rotates in a fixed order, slot by slot, and the other nodes check and vote on the proposed block. Candidate block comes from the designated leader. Advantages: simple, deterministic, fair, no wasted power, fast finality on a small known network. Disadvantages: a faulty or offline leader stalls its slot, the next leader is predictable so it is easy to target, one bad node per turn limits throughput, and alone it gives no Sybil resistance so it must be paired with known identities.

figure.aria: Three nodes draw random waits of four, two and seven seconds, so node B has the shortest wait and proposes the block at two seconds.

chapters.example: Three validators draw waits of 4 s, 2 s and 7 s. The shortest is B at 2 s, so B proposes, and the others verify its proof of wait before accepting the block. In a round robin chain with 3 validators, slots of 5 s each, and slot 1 given to A, the proposer of slot n is ((n − 1) mod 3) + 1. Slot 7 gives (7 − 1) mod 3 = 0, so validator A proposes again, at time (7 − 1) × 5 = 30 s.
chapters.trap: Saying PoET needs no trust at all, or that round robin alone survives Byzantine nodes.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 for permissioned versus permissionless consensus; 3.5 for how stake-based turns work.
chapters.leave: Hyperledger Sawtooth's full setup to Unit 6; Raft and Tendermint internals to an elective course.

chapters.idea: A fork is a divergence in the chain, and whether it is soft or hard depends on whether old nodes still accept the new blocks.
chapters.depth: Definition and causes: rule upgrades, bug fixes, disagreement among developers and miners, and ordinary block latency producing temporary forks (two miners find a block at the same height). Soft fork: the new rules are a strict subset of the old ones, so new blocks are still valid to old nodes; backward compatible; needs a majority of hash power or stake to enforce. Hard fork: the new rules are incompatible, old nodes reject new blocks, so the chain splits permanently into two and each side keeps its own history and its own coin. Examples: SegWit as a soft fork and Bitcoin Cash as a hard fork in 2017; Ethereum's 2016 hard fork that produced Ethereum Classic. Confirmation depth protects against a temporary fork. Reorg depth. Do not confuse a fork with a stale block.

figure.aria: From one block, a soft fork keeps all nodes on a single chain, while a hard fork splits into an old chain and a new chain that reject each other.

chapters.example: The rule says a block must be at most 1 MB. Upgrade one lowers the limit to 0.5 MB: a 0.5 MB block is still valid under the old 1 MB rule, so old nodes accept it and no split occurs; that is a soft fork. Upgrade two raises the limit to 2 MB: a 2 MB block is invalid for old nodes, so they reject it and keep building the old chain; that is a hard fork. If 85% of hash power runs the new rule and 15% runs the old, the new chain grows at 85% of the network rate and the old chain at 15%, and each chain retargets its own difficulty after 2016 blocks.
chapters.trap: Saying a soft fork can never split the chain at all, or calling an ordinary stale block a hard fork.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 and 3.5 for the two mechanisms that forks split along; Unit 1 for block structure.
chapters.leave: SegWit transaction formats and the DAO fork details to Units 4 and 5; side chains and the GHOST protocol to Unit 5.
